title: The true scholar
hook: the true pandit is one who instructs his own mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 9: the true aparas, untouched by falsehood, seeing God in all. Your line was true, not titled. Today, ashtpadi nine takes up another title: the scholar. Day four hundred seventy-one.

A friend can win any argument and still can't stop checking his phone at dinner. A brilliant expert gives wonderful advice and never takes any of it. Knowing a lot and being changed by what you know are two very different things. A student crams for an exam and forgets it by the next term. A teacher explains patience beautifully and loses her temper at the photocopier. In the Guru's day, the pandit was the learned one, the scholar who knew the old texts and taught them. Ashtpadi nine asks: who does the true pandit teach first?
screen: `WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.` → `NEVER TAKES HIS OWN ADVICE.` → `WHO DOES THE PANDIT TEACH FIRST?`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: so pandit jo man parbodhai. That one is a pandit who instructs his own mind. Parbodh means to awaken, to teach, to bring to understanding. The first student is the self. The next line: he searches for the Lord's Name within his own soul. Then: he drinks the sweet essence of the Name, and by that pandit's teaching the world lives. Then a line that tells you this pandit is not rejecting learning: he understands the root of the old scriptures, and sees the large hidden in the small. So the true scholar still reads. But the reading has gone somewhere. It's gone inward first, and come back out as a life. And then a line with real weight in a society ordered by caste: he gives teaching to all four castes. Chahu varnaa: all four. The stanza's ideal scholar teaches everyone. Sikh practice carries that on: the Guru Granth Sahib, written in Gurmukhi script in the spoken languages of its time, is read aloud to anyone who walks into the gurdwara. The stanza ends with Nanak bowing, forever, to that kind of pandit. So the order matters. Teach your own mind first. Then, and only then, your teaching might keep the world alive. Notice this isn't anti-intellectual. Sikh tradition honors its scholars, poets and scribes. It's about which direction the learning flows.
screen: `SO PANDIT: HE TEACHES HIS OWN MIND.` · `SEARCHING THE NAME WITHIN.` · `HE TEACHES ALL FOUR CASTES.` · `INWARD FIRST, THEN OUT AS A LIFE.` · then, large: `TEACH YOUR OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The practice: teach yourself one thing. Pick a piece of advice you often give other people. Slow down. Drink water. Don't take it personally. Say it now, silently, to yourself, as if you were the student and also the teacher. Then ask your mind, kindly: did you hear that? Sit with the answer, whatever it is, without scolding. Breathe in: the teacher speaks. Breathe out: the student listens. If you pray, you can ask for an awakened mind. The bell holds the time.
Pandit, a learned person. So pandit jo man parbodhai: the real pandit is the one who instructs his own mind, and then teaches everyone.
Your line: teach your own mind. Today, before you give anyone advice, try it on yourself first, once. Day four hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs value study of Gurbani through katha and personal reading, and read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that learning should first change the learner.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pandit, a learned person; ashtpadi nine names the true one as the one who teaches his own mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: a true scholar is the one who knows the most.
what it means: the true pandit teaches his own mind first, then everyone, of every caste.
what a scholar hears: parbodh (Sanskrit prabodha, awakening); the stanza's 'chahu varnaa kau de updes' opens sacred teaching to all four varnas.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS date fix: 'sixteenth-century India' removed (Sukhmani is usually dated c. 1602, as day 470's audit noted); 'read aloud in Punjabi script' corrected to Gurmukhi script in the spoken languages of its time; hook no longer opens 'Everyone knows'; 'Sikh history is full of' softened.

Pauri paraphrased: so pandit jo man parbodhai / raam naam aatam meh sodhai / raam naam saar ras peevai / us pandit kai updes jag jeevai / ... bed puraan simrit boojhai mool / sookham meh jaanai asthool / chahu varnaa kau de updes / Nanak us pandit kau sadaa ades. Confirm pauri number and lines.
Framing of pandits in the Guru's day is meant to be respectful; Keeper (and possibly a Hindu reviewer) should check.
'Sacred learning often kept within one group' is a general historical statement; confirm wording.
